description: Tasks for when a parent is sick, declining, or in hospice. Death is expected but hasn't happened. Focus: Do everything that requires them to be alive or lucid.

tasks.title: Find out if Power of Attorney exists
tasks.description: Without POA, you cannot make decisions or access anything if they become incapacitated. This is THE most time-sensitive legal task. Ask directly or check with their attorney.
tasks.why_now: Must be done while they are mentally competent. If no POA exists, an elder law attorney can create one quickly—but only while they're lucid.
tasks.why_it_matters: Power of Attorney allows you to manage finances and make healthcare decisions if they become unable to. Without it, you may need expensive court proceedings (guardianship/conservatorship) to help.
tips: Ask directly: 'Do you have a power of attorney set up? Who is it?'
There are two types: financial POA and healthcare POA (or healthcare proxy)
Check with their attorney if they have one
The person must be mentally competent to sign these documents
If no POA exists and they're willing, an elder law attorney can set this up quickly

tasks.title: Understand their care wishes / advance directive
tasks.description: DNR? Comfort care vs. intervention? Hospice should have asked, but confirm. This guides medical decisions and prevents family conflict.
tasks.why_now: Must happen while they can communicate. These wishes need to be documented and shared with medical team.
tasks.why_it_matters: Clear advance directives prevent family conflicts and ensure your parent's wishes are followed, even if they can't communicate. Doctors need this guidance.
tips: Ask about DNR (Do Not Resuscitate) preferences
Discuss comfort care vs. aggressive treatment
Ask about organ and tissue donation wishes
Make sure their doctor has a copy of any advance directive
Hospice can help facilitate these conversations

tasks.title: Find out if they have a will
tasks.description: Ask directly: 'Do you have a will? Where is it? Who's the executor?' 10x easier to ask now than to hunt for later.
tasks.why_now: They can tell you where it is and explain their wishes. If no will exists and they're lucid, a simple one can be done quickly.
tasks.why_it_matters: The will names the executor and contains burial wishes. Without one, state law decides everything—which may not match their wishes and can cause family conflict.
tips: Ask directly: 'Do you have a will? Where is it?'
Ask who the executor is—this person will be in charge
Check with their attorney if they have one
If no will exists, simple wills can be done online (LegalZoom, Trust & Will) for a few hundred dollars
A will can be updated as long as they're mentally competent

tasks.title: Have the funeral wishes conversation
tasks.description: Burial or cremation? Cemetery preference? Religious service? Organ donation? This conversation is hard but prevents agonizing guesswork later.
tasks.why_now: Only they can tell you what they actually want. Write down what they say so you don't have to remember.
tasks.why_it_matters: Knowing their wishes removes the burden of guessing during the most painful time. It also honors them by ensuring things are done the way they wanted.
tips: Start gently: 'I want to make sure we honor what you want'
Ask about burial vs. cremation, cemetery preferences
Ask about religious service, music, readings, who they'd want involved
Write down or record their wishes so you remember details
It's okay to have this conversation in pieces over time

tasks.title: Gather important documents with their help
tasks.description: Will, POA, insurance policies, deeds, account info, passwords. They can tell you where things are. Make copies. Find the safe deposit box key.
tasks.why_now: They can show you where things are and explain what they have. This becomes a scavenger hunt after they're gone.
tasks.why_it_matters: Searching for documents while grieving is exhausting. Knowing where things are now saves enormous stress later.
tips: Ask: 'Where do you keep important papers?'
Check for a safe deposit box—where's the key and which bank?
Look for a fireproof safe at their home
Get contact info for their attorney, accountant, financial advisor
Take photos of document locations so you remember

tasks.title: Understand their financial picture
tasks.description: What accounts exist? What bills are on autopay? Any debts? You need a rough map—not a forensic audit. Ask them to walk you through it.
tasks.why_now: They can explain their finances to you directly. After death, you'll be piecing together clues from mail and statements.
tasks.why_it_matters: After someone dies, you need to find and notify all financial institutions. Knowing what exists makes this much easier.
tips: Ask: 'Which banks do you use?' 'Do you have any investment accounts?'
Check if they have a list of accounts somewhere
Ask about debts: mortgage, car loans, credit cards
Don't forget retirement accounts (401k, IRA, pension)
Ask about automatic payments—mortgage, utilities, insurance

tasks.title: Ask about life insurance
tasks.description: 'Do you have life insurance? Through work? Where are the policies?' Write down company names and policy numbers if possible.
tasks.why_now: They can tell you what policies exist. Many people forget about old policies or employer coverage.
tasks.why_it_matters: Life insurance can provide funds for funeral costs and support survivors. Many policies go unclaimed because families don't know they exist.
tips: Ask directly: 'Do you have any life insurance?'
Ask about employer-provided life insurance (current or past employers)
Check if there's coverage through professional associations or credit cards
Write down company names and policy numbers
Ask where the policy documents are kept

tasks.title: Get added to key accounts or document access
tasks.description: With POA, you can access accounts. Without it, ask if they'll add you to checking or share login info. After death, accounts freeze until probate clears.
tasks.why_now: This can only be done while they're alive and willing. After death, individual accounts freeze and require legal process to access.
tasks.why_it_matters: Joint account holders can continue using accounts. Without joint access or POA, you may not be able to pay their bills or access funds for months.
tips: If you have POA, you can be added as authorized on accounts
Consider being added as a joint owner on checking (for bill paying)
Ask if they use a password manager or where passwords are kept
Email access is critical—it's used to find and recover other accounts
Some services offer legacy contacts (Apple, Facebook, Google)

tasks.title: Prepare the surviving parent
tasks.description: If applicable: Does your other parent know how to pay bills? Access accounts? Many couples divided responsibilities for decades.
tasks.why_now: Gentle conversations now prevent crisis later. The surviving spouse will be grieving—better to prepare them now.
tasks.why_it_matters: Many spouses divided financial responsibilities for decades. The surviving parent may not know passwords, account numbers, or even where the checkbook is.
tips: Ask if both parents know how to access bank accounts
Make sure both know where important documents are
Discuss ongoing bills and who pays them
Consider if they'll need help with tasks their spouse handles
This can be a sensitive conversation—approach gently

tasks.title: Take care of yourself
tasks.description: Anticipatory grief is real grief. Find someone to talk to. Take breaks from caregiving. You can't help anyone if you collapse.
tasks.why_now: You're carrying a lot. The practical tasks will still be there tomorrow. Your wellbeing matters.
tasks.why_it_matters: You can't pour from an empty cup. Taking care of yourself isn't selfish—it's necessary to be present for your parent and handle what's ahead.
tips: Anticipatory grief can be as intense as grief after death
It's okay to feel relief alongside sadness—that's normal
Consider talking to a therapist or grief counselor now
Lean on friends and family for support
Take breaks when you need them—you don't have to be present every moment
